subject: Thermodynamics
summary: available and unavailable energy, exergy of heat, closed systems and flow streams, irreversibility (Gouy–Stodola) and second-law efficiency, the Maxwell relations, Clapeyron and Clausius–Clapeyron equations, c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> relations and the Joule–Thomson coefficient

questions.text: Heat Q is received reversibly at a constant temperature T, as shown on the T–s diagram; the environment is at T₀. Which statement about the shaded areas is correct?
opts: X is the unavailable energy and Y the available energy
X is the available energy and Y the unavailable energy
X + Y is the available energy
Y is the irreversibility of the process
questions.ans: (B) X is the available energy and Y the unavailable energy
solution: Concept: Of heat Q received at T, the most that can be converted to work is Q(1 − T₀/T), the Carnot fraction with the environment as sink.
Area X (between T and T₀) = (T − T₀)Δs = available energy
Area Y (below T₀) = T₀Δs = unavailable energy, rejected to the environment even by a reversible engine.
Exam tip: Unavailable energy = T₀ × ΔS of the heat source; it is never zero unless T₀ = 0 K.

questions.text: 2000 kJ of heat is supplied from a reservoir at 800 K; the surroundings are at 300 K. The available energy (in kJ) is ______
solution: Concept: AE = Q(1 − T₀/T) for heat drawn from a reservoir at constant T.
Exam tip: This is the work a Carnot engine would give using the surroundings as its sink.

questions.text: 1000 kJ of heat flows from a reservoir at 1200 K to a reservoir at 600 K. With the surroundings at 300 K, the loss of available energy (in kJ) is ______
solution: Concept: Available energy before: Q(1 − T₀/T₁); after: Q(1 − T₀/T₂). The difference is T₀Sgen.
Exam tip: Heat 'degrades' when it flows down a temperature gradient: same energy, less exergy.

questions.text: The Maxwell relation obtained from the Gibbs function (dg = v dp − s dT) is
solution: Concept: For an exact differential dz = M dx + N dy, (∂M/∂y)x = (∂N/∂x)y.
With dg = v dp − s dT: (∂v/∂T)<sub>p</sub> = −(∂s/∂p)<sub>T</sub>
So (∂s/∂p)T = −(∂v/∂T)p.
Exam tip: Memory aid: the four relations come from du, dh, da, dg; the minus sign appears for du and dg.

questions.text: 3 kg of air (c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K) is cooled at constant pressure from 800 K to the surroundings temperature of 300 K. The available energy of the heat given out (in kJ, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: For a finite source the temperature falls as heat leaves, so AE = Q − T₀ΔS (not Q(1 − T₀/T)).
Exam tip: Using the initial temperature 800 K in the Carnot factor would give 942 kJ, an overestimate.

questions.text: A real gas is throttled through a valve and its temperature falls. At that state its Joule–Thomson coefficient μ = (∂T/∂p)<sub>h</sub> is
opts: positive, and the state lies below the inversion curve
questions.ans: (C) positive, and the state lies below the inversion curve
solution: Concept: Throttling is isenthalpic and the pressure falls (dp < 0).
A temperature drop (dT < 0) with dp < 0 means μ = dT/dp > 0.
μ > 0 inside (below) the inversion curve: positive. This is how gases are liquefied in the Linde process.
Exam tip: Ideal gas: μ = 0. Hydrogen and helium at room temperature have μ < 0 (they warm on throttling) and must be pre-cooled.

questions.text: At 200 °C, saturated water has v<sub>f</sub> = 0.001157 m³/kg, v<sub>g</sub> = 0.12736 m³/kg and h<sub>fg</sub> = 1940.7 kJ/kg. The slope dp/dT of the saturation curve at 200 °C from the Clapeyron equation (in kPa/K, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Clapeyron: dp/dT = hfg/(T vfg), exact for any phase change.
Exam tip: kJ/m³ = kPa, so with h in kJ/kg and v in m³/kg the slope comes out directly in kPa/K.

questions.text: Which statement about the specific heats of a substance is correct?
opts: c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R for every substance
c<sub>p</sub> < c<sub>v</sub> for water between 0 °C and 4 °C
c<sub>p</sub> = c<sub>v</sub> for an ideal gas
c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R for an ideal gas and is nearly zero for liquids and solids
questions.ans: (D) c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = R for an ideal gas and is nearly zero for liquids and solids
solution: Concept: General relation: cp − cv = Tvβ²/κ.
Ideal gas: β = 1/T, κ = 1/p → c<sub>p</sub> − c<sub>v</sub> = pv/T = R.
Liquids and solids have very small β, so c<sub>p</sub> ≈ c<sub>v</sub>, which is why a single 'c' is quoted for them.
So the correct choice is (D).
Exam tip: Since κ > 0 always, cp can never be less than cv.

questions.text: Air (an ideal gas, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K) is throttled adiabatically from 800 kPa to 200 kPa. With T₀ = 300 K, the exergy destroyed per kg of air (in kJ/kg, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Throttling an ideal gas: h and T stay constant, but entropy rises.
s<sub>gen</sub> = R ln(p₁/p₂) = 0.287 ln 4 = 0.39787 kJ/kg·K
Exam tip: No energy is lost in a valve, but exergy is — that is why expansion valves are replaced by turbines in large plants.

questions.text: A refrigerator keeps a cold space at −20 °C and rejects heat to a kitchen at 30 °C. Its actual COP is 2.5. Its second-law efficiency is about
solution: Concept: ηII = COP/COPrev.
COP<sub>rev</sub> = T<sub>L</sub>/(T<sub>H</sub> − T<sub>L</sub>) = 253.15/50 = 5.06
Exam tip: Second-law efficiency compares with the best possible device between the same temperatures; it can never exceed 1.

questions.text: Air (c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K) is compressed in the adiabatic steady-flow compressor shown from 100 kPa, 300 K to 600 kPa, 550 K. With T₀ = 300 K, the exergy destroyed per kg of air (in kJ/kg, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Adiabatic device: sgen = s₂ − s₁; Gouy–Stodola: i = T₀sgen.
Actual work = 1.005 × 250 = 251.2 kJ/kg, so about 11 % of the input is destroyed.
Exam tip: The minimum (reversible) work = actual work − T₀sgen for an adiabatic compressor.

questions.text: For a closed system that can exchange heat only with the atmosphere at T₀ and p₀ and ends at T₀ and p₀, the maximum useful work obtainable equals the decrease in its
solution: Concept: Useful work excludes the work done against the atmosphere, p₀ΔV.
At constant T₀ and p₀, W<sub>useful,max</sub> = −ΔG = G₁ − G₂.
At constant T and V (no atmospheric work), the maximum work is −ΔA (Helmholtz function A = U − TS).
So the answer is the Gibbs function.
Exam tip: Helmholtz → constant T and V; Gibbs → constant T and p.

questions.text: Air flows steadily at 500 K and 400 kPa with negligible velocity. With the dead state at 300 K and 100 kPa (c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K), its specific flow exergy (in kJ/kg, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Flow exergy ψ = (h − h₀) − T₀(s − s₀) + V²/2 + gz.
Exam tip: Flow exergy uses h (it includes flow work); non-flow exergy uses u + p₀v.

questions.text: Using the relation (∂u/∂v)<sub>T</sub> = T(∂p/∂T)<sub>v</sub> − p for a van der Waals gas, (p + a/v²)(v − b) = RT, the value of (∂u/∂v)<sub>T</sub> is
solution: Concept: From the van der Waals equation, p = RT/(v − b) − a/v², so (∂p/∂T)v = R/(v − b).
T(∂p/∂T)v − p = RT/(v − b) − [RT/(v − b) − a/v²] = a/v²
For an ideal gas (a = 0) it is zero: u depends on T only (Joule's law).
Exam tip: Internal energy of a real gas rises with volume at fixed T because molecules move apart against attraction.

questions.text: Water boils at 100 °C at 101.325 kPa, with h<sub>fg</sub> = 2257 kJ/kg (assume constant) and R = 0.4615 kJ/kg·K for the vapour. Using the Clausius–Clapeyron equation, the boiling point at a hill station where the pressure is 70 kPa is closest to
solution: Concept: Clausius–Clapeyron (ideal vapour, vf neglected): ln(p₂/p₁) = (hfg/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂).
Exam tip: Lower pressure → lower boiling point; this is why a pressure cooker (higher p) cooks faster.
